name: Swahili
notes: Swahili (Kiswahili). Bantu lingua franca of East Africa; official in Tanzania, Kenya, Uganda and the DRC. KEY FEATURES: (1) FIVE-VOWEL SYSTEM a/e/i/o/u, of the cross-linguistically ordinary evenly-dispersed type (Maddieson 2003 §2 reports Nchimbi's 1997 formant study placing Swahili with Xhosa, Spanish and Hawaiian) — written here /a ɛ i ɔ u/. (2) IMPLOSIVE VOICED STOPS: the voiced stop series is implosive [ɓ ɗ ʄ ɠ]; Polomé (1967: 38-40), reported in Alsamaani (2023) Table 3, gives four laryngeal categories of Swahili stops and lists /b ɓ d ɗ g ɠ/ alongside /p pʰ t tʰ k kʰ/. The pulmonic plosive is kept as a second candidate for Arabic and English loans. (3) POST-NASAL PLOSIVES: after a homorganic nasal the voiced stop is a pulmonic plosive, not an implosive (Hayward, Omar & Goesche 1989 on Kimvita, reported in Alsamaani 2023), which is why <mb nd nj ng> keep [mb nd ndʒ ŋɡ]. (4) FLAP /ɾ/: <r> is a flap, listed as such in Alsamaani (2023) Table 3. (5) SYLLABIC NASALS: <m n> before a consonant letter form a syllable of their own (mtu [m̩tu]) — declared on before_consonant, so <m> before a vowel (mama) stays plain [m]. (6) NG vs NG': <ng'> is [ŋ] and <ng> is [ŋɡ]. (7) ARABIC LOAN GRAPHEMES: <dh th gh> = [ð θ ɣ] and <kh> = [x] (Awino et al. 2022 §2: '/kh/ = kheri'; Mgullu 1999, cited there, lists /x (kh)/ in the consonant inventory). (8) NO TONE. NOT MODELLED, deliberately: Swahili has an aspiration contrast /p pʰ t tʰ k kʰ/ (Polomé 1967: 39-40 treats the aspirates as independent phonemes) which the orthography does not write, so no grapheme can predict it; and vowel length arising from vowel sequences is likewise unwritten.

sources.notes: Surveys the Kiswahili phoneme inventories of Ashton 1951 through Akidah 2013; source for <kh> = [x] in Arabic loans.

sources.author: Maddieson, I.
sources.title: The sounds of the Bantu languages (Chapter 2 of The Bantu Languages)
sources.notes: Places Swahili's five-vowel system with the evenly-dispersed /i e a o u/ type, and describes implosives as usual in the eastern coastal Bantu area.

stress.notes: Swahili (Standard, as spoken in Tanzania/Kenya) has regular penultimate stress in native vocabulary. Loanwords may carry final stress but those are a minority. Source: Nurse & Hinnebusch (1993), Swahili and Sabaki; Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swahili_phonology

ancestors.notes: Arabic adstrate: the dominant contact layer of the Swahili coast — a very large share of the lexicon.
English adstrate: colonial and modern loanwords.
Persian adstrate: early Indian-Ocean trade vocabulary.
